title: Optimal general-domain CSP approximation under Unique Games hardness
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture and \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\), determine up to universal constant factors the optimal expected approximation ratio \(\rho(k,d)\) for every fixed arity \(k\ge2\) and domain size \(d\ge2\). The source proposes the scale \[q(k,d)=\frac{\max\{k,\log d\}}{d^{k-1}},\] which is retained as context rather than assumed to equal the answer.
why: The question asks how arity and the number of labels jointly control the best efficient approximation of arbitrary local constraints. Matching bounds would explain the transition between Boolean-like behavior and large-domain instances, with consequences for the quantitative strength of probabilistically checkable proofs.
status_note: A user-authorized conditional quantitative variant of the source’s general-domain optimality question. The checked bounds and Boolean-only preprint claims do not determine the full joint scale. The model and explicit hardness hypotheses were reviewed on 13 September 2026; new preprint proofs were not independently verified.
review_note: Completed individual source and formulation review on 13 September 2026; see statement_review and research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: The arity-sensitive algorithm matches known hardness when arity is at least the domain size.
The logarithmic-domain approximation and near-matching UGC-hardness improve the large-domain regime.
The survey asks whether the combined approximation scale is optimal across the full parameter range.
Two preprints claim improvements to the leading constant for the Boolean case; they do not resolve the general-domain question.

sentences: The input lists local constraints on variables with a finite common label domain.
The task maximizes the number of satisfied constraints using randomized polynomial time for each fixed arity and domain size.
The target is the best expected approximation ratio, compared across both parameters with universal constants.
The chosen hardness framework assumes Unique Games hardness and that NP is not contained in BPP.
Known matching regimes and recent Boolean leading-constant claims do not determine the full general-domain scale.

definitions: An instance has an explicit finite list of variables with values in \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\), and an explicit finite list of constraints. Each constraint names at most \(k\) distinct variables and gives the full Boolean truth table of its predicate on those variables. A repeated constraint counts separately. All variables, indices, delimiters and table entries count in the input bit length \(L\); there is no succinct predicate circuit or implicit list. The value of an assignment is the number of satisfied constraints, and \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) is the maximum value. For fixed \((k,d)\), an admissible algorithm is a uniform fair-coin Turing machine that outputs an assignment and halts within \(C_{k,d}(L+1)^{a_{k,d}}\) steps on every input and random tape, including output time. Its code and constants may depend on the fixed parameters, but not on the instance. Define \(\rho(k,d)\) as the supremum of \(r\in[0,1]\) for which some admissible algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{val}(A(I))]\ge r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) on every instance; zero-optimum instances impose no additional ratio condition. The supremum is not presumed attained. Logarithms in \(q\) are natural. A constant-factor answer consists of a positive function \(g(k,d)\) and one \(C\ge1\) such that \(C^{-1}g(k,d)\le\rho(k,d)\le Cg(k,d)\) for all \(k,d\ge2\). No hidden constant may depend on either parameter. Here the Unique Games Conjecture means: for every rational \(0<\eta,\gamma<1/2\), there is a fixed label count \(R\ge2\) for which it is NP-hard to distinguish unique-game instances of optimum satisfied fraction at least \(1-\eta\) from those of optimum at most \(\gamma\). A unique-game instance is an explicitly listed finite bipartite multigraph with at least one edge, a label in \([R]\) at each vertex, and a permutation \(\pi_e:[R]\to[R]\) at each oriented edge; an edge is satisfied when its endpoint labels obey that permutation. The objective is the fraction of satisfied edges, counting multiplicity. NP-hardness of this promise problem means that every language with polynomial-time verifiable polynomial-length witnesses has a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction mapping members to the first promise and nonmembers to the second. BPP consists of languages decided by a uniform randomized polynomial-time machine with error at most \(1/3\) on every input. The additional assumption \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BPP}\) makes the NP-hardness premise exclude bounded-error randomized polynomial-time decision procedures. Both assumptions and the fixed-parameter algorithm convention are explicit editorial choices.
answer_criterion: Supply a positive comparison function and a Lean proof, conditional only on the two stated hypotheses, of both universal constant-factor bounds for the entire arity/domain range. A ratio established for each fixed parameter with uncontrolled parameter-dependent comparison constants does not suffice. Bounds only for Boolean domains or only for one parameter regime do not determine this target. The answer concerns a supremum of achievable expected ratios and does not require an optimum-attaining algorithm. Numerical 0.01 tolerance does not apply to the asymptotic scale.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether the combined arity-and-domain approximation scale is optimal. The authorized variant makes the hardness assumptions and the dependence of algorithms on fixed parameters explicit.
The checked primary papers identify \(k\ge d\) as a regime of matching bounds. The concluding survey sentence reverses that inequality; the card follows the primary theorem statements.
The 2016 paper gives improved bounds for large domains, while the August 2026 preprints concern the Boolean leading constant. Neither supplies matching dependence over the full two-parameter range.
